name: CrohnSight
problem: Reading a capsule-endoscopy study means checking tens of thousands of small-bowel frames by eye. Crohn's lesions are small and easy to miss.
approach: An ensemble of 10 EfficientNet-B2 models (5 folds × 2 seeds) at the native 320 px finds lesions in 7 classes, grades severity in 4 tiers and draws a heat-map over each lesion. It is exported to ONNX and runs offline on an ordinary CPU. Add-ons cover ulcerative-colitis Mayo grading and flare-risk forecasting.
features: Lesion Analyzer: 7 lesion classes, a severity tier, a heat-map and how many of the 10 models agree
Study Triage: a folder or .zip of frames ranked most suspicious first, with a Balanced or Screening cut-off
Video Scan of your own capsule video, plus 43 Kvasir studies already scanned offline
Ulcerative-colitis grader (Mayo 0–3) and a flare-risk forecaster on HMP2 patient timelines
Tested untouched on Kvasir-Capsule (Norway, 47,238 frames) and SEE-AI (Japan)
FastAPI and onnxruntime on CPU with a pre-built Next.js UI and Docker: no GPU or PyTorch needed
limits: Research prototype, not a medical device. Telling a whole lesion video from a lesion-free one is near chance (study AUROC 0.57). The README reports this openly.
team: With Hil Kalathiya and Chetan Gadhiya · PDEU minor project, guided by Prof. Dr. Babalu Kumar Singh

name: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator
problem: Enterprise questions mix document lookups, database queries and actions such as sending email. A single RAG chain answers them badly or unsafely.
approach: A LangGraph Supervisor → Worker → Validator graph routes each query to Corrective RAG, NL-to-SQL, a human-in-the-loop email tool or chat. Retrieval is hybrid (Qdrant dense + BM25), reranked with a CrossEncoder and expanded from 200- to 800-token parent chunks, with an LLM grader that rewrites weak queries. A semantic cache, prompt-injection guards and Fernet encryption protect it.
features: A Supervisor picks one of four routes: Corrective RAG, NL-to-SQL, an email tool or chat
A Validation agent re-grounds every answer as {answer, source, confidence}
An LLM grades each retrieved chunk and rewrites weak queries, at most 2 rounds
Semantic cache in Qdrant (cosine ≥ 0.96) answers repeated questions without the pipeline
Email only through Draft → Confirm → Execute, with a domain allow-list and an hourly cap
Groq, OpenAI, Anthropic or Bedrock with automatic failover; read-only SQL; 15 pytest tests

name: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent
problem: Cleaning a messy table takes many small, ordered decisions. Can an agent learn them, and can its score be checked honestly?
approach: An OpenEnv environment over pandas tables with reproducible (task, seed) episodes and a hidden clean ground truth. Potential-based reward shaping makes going in circles worthless, and a separate grader scores the final table. The benchmark compares a PPO agent (400k steps, exported to NumPy), a zero-shot Llama 3.1 8B agent and rule-based baselines, served over FastAPI and WebSocket with a Gradio demo.
features: Three tasks: easy (40 rows), medium (60 rows + duplicates), hard (100 rows, every kind of mess)
Nine actions: fill, dedupe, standardise categories, cast types, fix dates, clip outliers and more
Invalid actions are not applied: the agent gets the reason in last_error and a small penalty
Grader: 0.6 cell accuracy + 0.2 row fidelity + 0.2 schema, revealed only when the episode ends
PPO on 8 parallel workers, validated on seeds 50–59 and tested on unseen seeds 0–9
97 tests, Ruff linting and a live Gradio demo on Hugging Face Spaces
limits: The data is synthetic, and Q is only a proxy for quality, which is why a separate grader exists.
team: With Chetan Gadhiya and Hil Kalathiya

name: Sleep-Consolidating LLM
problem: A language model learns nothing from what happens after training. An agent can keep notes, but the model itself either never absorbs them or, once fine-tuned on them, forgets older skills. Can it "sleep": turn a day's notes into weights without losing what it already knew?
approach: Each simulated day a 4-bit Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads documents from a seeded synthetic world of names it cannot know (about 20% of facts are later updated) and writes atomic notes. At night it dreams: grounded question-answer pairs (answer-first), paraphrases and counterfactuals, de-duplicated and selected for diversity. One rank-16 QLoRA adapter is trained on a mix of 40% dreams from earlier nights, 20% ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and GSM8K train items and 40% new dreams, with a KL-to-base penalty on the replay part. QA is scored on held-out phrasings with no notebook.

metric.label: recall of earlier days' facts after 5 nights, no notebook (naive training: 0.035)

limits: Indicative only: 3 seeds, 5 nights, a 0.5B model and roughly 50 to 100 questions per cell. Training on dreams at all raises perplexity above the base model. Whether one rank-16 adapter holds about 1,500 facts is untested; a 30-night run is in progress. The earlier replay design forgot most earlier days (0.07 at day 5).

a line chart of a score
name: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation
problem: Fault-tolerant quantum algorithms are priced in qubits and Toffoli gates. Google Quantum AI's Kaggle competition asks for smaller circuits for three workloads: a 1/√x phase for fusion energy, a Reed-Solomon decoder for optimisation and FeMoCo chemistry loaders. An official verifier checks every submission on fresh random inputs, and the score is the geometric mean of the three cost reductions.
approach: Own circuits for two of the three tasks, built with kickmix and checked with the official verifier logic. invsqrt: a table-based piecewise-quadratic design (192-entry QROM, binary shift count, barrel normaliser), lazy register allocation, narrow-window multiplies, measurement-based lookup erase and dead-gate removal checked over all 3.13M inputs. dqi: a tower-field GF(2^12) inverse (315 to 91 Toffolis), a 54-AND multiplier and a statistical dead-gate remover. Multi-core verifier runners for Windows run the full checks.

metric.label: lower cost on invsqrt, own circuit (2,076,774 → 323,146)

metrics: 136 qubits, 2,125 Toffolis; full 64-shot check on all 3.13M inputs passed
1.64× (1,869 qubits; about 30 failures in 102,400 shots, R 1.276)
limits: The leaderboard's top scores come from public circuits of other participants. Re-verifying and submitting one such public stack scored 33.17 on Kaggle, but that is their work, credited in the repo, not mine. My own circuits reach about 2.2 and the chemistry task is untouched (1.0×). The dqi figure depends on a few decoder failures that vary with the grader's random draw. The code is not public.
code: The code is not public; the project is documented on the Kaggle competition page.
team: Solo entry · public work of other participants credited

visual: a Christmas scene with Santa Claus
name: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator
problem: For each of 1,000 puzzles a calculator with 48 registers starts from a few numbers and must produce every one of several huge targets (up to about 10^18) using + − × and exact division. The score is the total number of instructions across all puzzles, lower is better. The sample submission needs 1,490,379.
approach: An exact referee re-implements the rules and replays every program. A Horner-style solver gives the baseline. A forward/backward dictionary beam search (meet-in-the-middle over 2 to 4M values), a value-DAG local search with register allocation and a C++ cone re-synthesiser then look for shorter programs, and a best-of merger replays banks of programs and keeps the shortest valid one per puzzle. A gap report shows about 80% of instructions build helper values and targets are mostly helper-op-helper.

metric.label: total instructions after merging public programs (sample: 1,490,379)

metrics: 0 instructions saved (beam, DAG search, cone re-synthesis up to 4 helpers)
limits: Nearly all of the gain over my own baseline comes from other participants' public programs, replayed through the exact referee and credited in the repo; my beam search, local search and cone re-synthesis found nothing shorter than the public frontier. The code is in a private repository.

name: Explainable Student Performance
problem: A model that predicts which students will struggle is only useful if teachers can see why it made each prediction.
approach: Pandera-validated data and a ColumnTransformer pipeline feed a benchmark of 9 models: linear, tree ensembles, XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, a PyTorch MLP, a PyTorch LSTM and FLAML AutoML. SHAP and LIME explain each prediction, and Spearman rank correlation measures how far the two explanations agree. MLflow tracks runs, FastAPI serves the model and Streamlit shows it.
features: FastAPI routes: /health, /models, /predict, /predict/{model} and /explain
SHAP beeswarm, bar and waterfall plots, with a Tree, Linear or Kernel explainer per model
LIME explanations saved as HTML and as normalised JSON
Pandera schema checks run before any cleaning or feature engineering
Metrics, training time and inference latency of every model logged to MLflow and a CSV
CI on GitHub Actions: Ruff, 17 pytest tests with coverage and a Docker build

name: DCGAN Reproducibility+
problem: The 2015 DCGAN is famously unstable, and most re-implementations show only a grid of blurry samples, never what the networks learned inside.
approach: Keeps Radford et al.'s all-convolutional architecture but swaps in an LSGAN loss, Spectral Normalization, a Xavier/Kaiming initialisation, discriminator dropout and label smoothing. A custom GANAnalyzer hooks into the layers to show learned filters, mid-layer feature maps and the separation of D(x) from D(G(z)).
features: Paper settings kept: 64×64 images, a 100-dim z, batch 128, Adam 2e-4 with β₁ 0.5, LeakyReLU 0.2
Label smoothing [0.1, 0.9] and discriminator dropout 0.3 keep D from getting over-confident
Sample grids every 5 epochs and latent-space walks between random z vectors
A 4-panel dashboard: loss curves, D filters, feature maps and real-vs-fake score histograms
Two notebooks: one trains, the other analyses the saved model without retraining
PAPER_COMPARISON.md explains every change from the 2015 paper and why it was made

metric.label: stability fixes over the 2015 paper, each documented

metrics: Filters, feature maps, D(x) vs D(G(z)) histograms
